newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Appetite seen good for Philippine bonds.
newsitem.headline: Appetite seen good for Philippine bonds.

text.p: Interest in Philippine bonds among prospective investors is high, but prospects for the longer end are still limited and problems remain, currency dealers said on Friday.

"In point of fact, the appetite is quite high. I think every emerging market portfolio needs to have a component in Philippine paper," Richard Shrieve, executive vice president at Bank of America in Hong Kong, told Reuters at an Asian-Pacific forex conference here.
But he added that things are still "in an early stage", and that difficulties linger.

Speakers at the two-day forex conference, which began on Wednesday, lauded growth in the Philippines, which has seen inflation fall to a low of 4.4 percent in September from double-digit numbers a year before. They also noted the vastly improved investment picture in the region.

"Currently there are no negative ratings outlooks anywhere in the area, and a distinctly positive outlook for some, including the Philippines," Jeremy Palmer, chairman of the Asia-Pacific region at ING Barings, told the conference.

In what may be an encouraging sign of things to come in the Philippine bond market, central bank governor Gabriel Singson announced on Thursday that he is considering a proposal to issue a 30-year dollar bond on the international market.
A lack of overall liquidity and a dearth of regular issues along the yield curve were cited by dealers as some of the main drawbacks of the Philippine debt market.
To date, the longest Philippine-peso denominated issue is the 10-year bond, first offered this past September.
Only one-year treasury bills were issued until 1994, at which point two-year notes were introduced. Five-year notes followed in 1995, and seven-year notes earlier this year.

An offer totaling $1.9 billion in uncollateralised fifteen- and twenty-year U.S. dollar bonds was proposed by the government, also in September, as an exchange for Philippine Brady Bonds. The Brady Bonds were issued in 1992 as part of the government's debt restructuring program.
Although dealers said the proposed 30-year bond was a step in the right direction, the consensus appeared to be that these bonds would find a cool reception.
"Right now, the market appetite and liquidity is still limited to the short end, mainly around one-two years," said Rafael Algarra, head of the money market desk at Standard Chartered Bank in Manila.

Algarra added that the small issue volume of longer maturities was definitely a problem. "Most of the longer end is being gobbled up by institutional investors, and the volume is so small that it can be easily absorbed by only one or two companies," he said.
Two billion pesos ($76.34 million) of ten-year bonds were offered in September.

Bank of America's Shrieve noted that he remains concerned about a number of factors, including the 20 percent withholding tax on Philippine investment earnings and the need to establish a solid sovereign market.
But he added: "Low U.S. interest rates will stimulate a good deal of supply from Asia, and there is still tremendous liquidity in the world market with little sign of oversupply."
Standard and Poor's gave the proposed 15- and 20-year bonds a BB rating in September, and said the ratings outlook was positive.
